name: GCP identity — projects/folders, service accounts, Workload Identity Federation from GitHub Actions, IAM conditions, no JSON keys
short_definition: The identity layer for a greenfield GCP footprint: an org/folder/project resource hierarchy that scopes IAM policy inheritance, user-managed service accounts that hold least-privilege roles, and Workload Identity Federation (WIF) that lets GitHub Actions (and other external OIDC-emitting workloads) exchange a short-lived GitHub OIDC token for a short-lived Google STS token — either directly (Direct WIF, principalSet) or via service-account impersonation — with zero downloaded JSON service-account keys ever created, stored, or rotated.
scope_in: Org/folder/project hierarchy design and IAM inheritance; service account creation, naming, and least-privilege role binding; Workload Identity Pools and Providers; attribute mapping and attribute conditions for GitHub Actions OIDC; Direct WIF vs impersonation-via-WIF; IAM Conditions (CEL) on role bindings; organization policies that ban service-account key creation; the google-github-actions/auth GitHub Action wiring.
scope_out: Runtime workload identity for GKE Pods (see gcp-gke-workload-identity if present — different mechanism from user OIDC federation); Cloud Run/Cloud Functions invoker IAM and per-service SA attachment (see gcp-cloud-run item); Supabase auth/RLS identity (owned by the supabase cluster); Vercel deployment identity and its own OIDC federation to GCP/AWS (owned by vercel cluster); secret storage mechanics in Secret Manager (see gcp-secret-manager item); billing/quota escalation workflows beyond the identity-relevant quotas listed here.
defaults: One GCP organization per company; folders per environment or business unit (e.g. `prod`, `staging`, `sandbox`) directly under the org, projects nested under environment folders — never flat projects at org root for anything beyond a personal sandbox.
One project per environment per product line minimum (e.g. `my-project-prod`, `my-project-staging`) so IAM, quotas, and billing don't bleed across environments.
Zero downloaded service-account JSON keys anywhere — CI, local dev, containers. Local dev uses `gcloud auth application-default login` (user credentials) or short-lived impersonation; CI uses WIF.

GitHub Actions authenticates via `google-github-actions/auth@v3` using Direct WIF (principalSet bound straight to IAM roles) for simple cases, or WIF + service-account impersonation when the target API requires a service-account identity (e.g. some Cloud Run deploy paths, Firebase Admin SDK which does not support WIF).

Every Workload Identity Pool has exactly one provider per external CI system per trust boundary (e.g. `github-actions` pool with one provider trusting `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`), and every provider has a mandatory attribute condition — never rely on attribute mapping alone.

Attribute conditions and IAM bindings reference numeric identifiers (`assertion.repository_id`, `repository_owner_id`, org number) rather than name-based fields (`repository`, `repository_owner`) to prevent typosquatting/renaming attacks.
One dedicated, narrowly-scoped service account per CI workflow / deployment target (e.g. `deploy-web-prod@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com`), never a shared 'ci-everything' service account.
Organization policy `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` are enforced org-wide (default for orgs created after 2024-05-03; explicitly set for older orgs).

Production deploy permissions gated with an IAM Condition restricting the WIF-derived principal to the `main`/`release` branch and to `pull_request` == false, so PR-triggered workflows can't deploy to prod.
IAM roles granted are predefined or custom least-privilege roles scoped at the project (or resource) level — never `roles/owner` or `roles/editor` bound to a CI service account.
decision_gates: Use Direct WIF (grant IAM roles straight to the `principalSet://...` mapped from GitHub OIDC claims) when the target Google API accepts federated principals directly and you want one fewer hop — simplest, fewest moving parts, no service account to rotate/manage.

Use WIF + service-account impersonation when the target integration requires a classic service-account identity (many Terraform providers, some client libraries, Firebase Admin SDK — which explicitly does not support WIF and needs a key or ADC through a supported path) or when you want a stable principal identity independent of pool/provider churn.

Use a Google-managed folder-level IAM binding (not per-project) when the same CI identity needs the same role across many projects in one folder — reduces binding sprawl, but only do this if the blast radius of that grant is genuinely folder-wide by design.

Do NOT use long-lived service-account JSON keys for GitHub Actions, ever, in this stack — this is a hard architectural rule, not a preference. If a vendor tool only supports key-file auth, isolate it in its own project with a scoped, monitored service account and treat the key as a rotated secret in Secret Manager, not a repo secret.

Do NOT use `repository`/`repository_owner` string attributes as the sole gate in an attribute condition for anything touching prod — use the numeric `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id` claims instead, since GitHub usernames and repo names can be renamed and reassigned.

Prefer Vercel's own OIDC-to-GCP federation (if the deploy originates from Vercel, not GitHub Actions) over funneling through a GitHub Actions intermediary — fewer hops, same no-keys guarantee; use GitHub Actions WIF when the pipeline itself lives in GitHub Actions (tests, IaC apply, container build/push).

Use a single shared 'infra' project with a dedicated WIF pool/provider for Terraform/OpenTofu apply identities, separate from the app-deploy pool/provider — infra-apply is higher privilege and should have its own trust boundary and audit trail.

Escalate to a full org-level Google Cloud landing zone (multiple folders, org policies, centralized logging project) only once you have more than a handful of projects or a compliance requirement; a single flat project is acceptable for an early-stage greenfield MVP with a clear migration plan.
do_dont: DO: create a distinct Workload Identity Pool provider per external CI/IdP system, with an explicit attribute condition on every provider.

DO: bind IAM roles to `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/attribute.repository_id/REPO_ID` (numeric) rather than name-based attributes for anything privileged.
DO: scope service accounts to a single workflow/purpose and grant only the exact predefined or custom roles that workflow needs.
DO: set org policies `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` at the organization node so no project can opt back into key-based auth silently.
DO: add an IAM Condition (or attribute condition) restricting production-impersonation grants to the release branch and to non-fork, non-PR event contexts.
DO: log and alert on Security Token Service (STS) token exchanges and IAM impersonation calls via Cloud Audit Logs data access logs.
DON'T: commit or generate any `*.json` file matching the service-account key shape (`"type": "service_account"`) anywhere in the repo, including fixtures or examples.

DON'T: set `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to point at a checked-in or CI-downloaded key file — ADC in CI should resolve through WIF-issued short-lived credentials injected by `google-github-actions/auth`.
DON'T: grant `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or org-level `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` to any CI-facing service account or principalSet.
DON'T: reuse one 'ci-deploy' service account across dev/staging/prod — cross-environment blast radius from a single compromised workflow.

DON'T: allow a WIF provider's attribute condition to accept any `repository_owner` without also constraining to a specific `repository_id`/`workflow_ref`, since a fork's workflow can otherwise mint tokens against your pool if the org-level condition is too loose.

DON'T: leave workload identity pools or providers with an empty/permissive attribute condition 'temporarily' — this is the single most common real-world WIF misconfiguration and is exploitable immediately.
config_skeleton:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. gcloud CLI — one-time WIF bootstrap (run by a human/admin, not CI)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PROJECT_ID="my-project-id"
PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe "$PROJECT_ID" --format='value(projectNumber)')
POOL_ID="github-actions"
PROVIDER_ID="my-repo-provider"
GITHUB_ORG="my-org"
GITHUB_REPO="my-org/my-repo"
SA_NAME="deploy-web-prod"
SA_EMAIL="${SA_NAME}@${PROJECT_ID}.iam.gserviceaccount.com"

# Create the pool (one per external IdP boundary; separate pools per env optional)
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create "$POOL_ID" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --location="global" \
  --display-name="GitHub Actions pool"

# Create the provider trusting GitHub's OIDC issuer, with attribute mapping
# NOTE: use numeric repository_id/repository_owner_id in the condition, not names.
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc "$PROVIDER_ID" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --location="global" \
  --workload-identity-pool="$POOL_ID" \
  --issuer-uri="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository_id=assertion.repository_id,attribute.repository_owner_id=assertion.repository_owner_id,attribute.ref=assertion.ref" \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.repository_owner_id=='00000000' && assertion.repository_id=='000000000'"

# Option A: Direct WIF — bind IAM role straight to the principalSet (no service account)
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" \
  --role="roles/run.developer" \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${POOL_ID}/attribute.repository_id/000000000" \
  --condition="expression=resource.name.startsWith('projects/${PROJECT_ID}/locations/us-central1/services/web'),title=scope-to-web-service"

# Option B: WIF + service-account impersonation (used when the target API needs a classic SA identity)
gcloud iam service-accounts create "$SA_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --display-name="CI deploy identity for web service (prod)"

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding "$SA_EMAIL" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser" \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${POOL_ID}/attribute.repository_id/000000000"

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" \
  --role="roles/run.developer" \
  --member="serviceAccount:${SA_EMAIL}"

# Org policy: hard-disable service-account key creation/upload (run once at org node)
gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce \
  iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation --organization=ORG_ID
gcloud resource-manager org-policies enable-enforce \
  iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload --organization=ORG_ID

# 3. GitHub Actions workflow — no JSON keys, short-lived STS token only

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
# name: deploy-prod
# on:

#     branches: [main]
# permissions:

#   id-token: write   # REQUIRED — mints the GitHub OIDC token; do not omit
# jobs:

#     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/checkout@v4

#         uses: google-github-actions/auth@v3
#         with:
#           project_id: 'my-project-id'
#           workload_identity_provider: 'projects/000000000000/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-actions/providers/my-repo-provider'
#           service_account: 'deploy-web-prod@my-project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com'  # omit for Direct WIF
#       - uses: google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v2
#       - run: gcloud run deploy web --project=my-project-id --region=us-central1 --image=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project-id/web/app:${{ github.sha }}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Local dev — never a key file
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# gcloud auth application-default login
# gcloud auth application-default login --impersonate-service-account=deploy-web-prod@my-project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com
failure_modes: Attribute condition on a WIF provider is missing, empty, or matches too broadly (e.g. only checks `attribute.repository_owner` string) — any fork, renamed repo, or unrelated workflow in the trusted org can mint a token and assume the mapped IAM role (confused-deputy escalation).
GitHub Actions workflow omits `permissions: id-token: write`, so no OIDC token is minted and the auth step fails at runtime — often only caught in CI, not locally.
A CI service account is granted a broad role (`roles/editor`) 'temporarily to unblock a deploy' and the grant is never walked back, becoming a standing over-privileged credential.

Firebase Admin SDK (or another WIF-incompatible library) is used inside a workflow that assumes WIF everywhere, silently falling back to requiring a downloaded key — reintroducing the exact risk the architecture was meant to eliminate.

Workload identity pool provider count creeps toward the 200-per-pool default limit when a new provider is created per repo instead of using one provider with repo-scoped attribute conditions — hits quota during a release freeze.
Project or folder count nested more than 10 levels deep, or a folder exceeds 300 direct child folders, silently blocking new project/folder creation during a reorg.

Attribute mapping references a claim name that changes between GitHub Actions OIDC token schema versions, breaking authentication for all workflows simultaneously after an unrelated GitHub platform change.

IAM Condition CEL expression grows past the practical complexity budget (Google recommends staying well under 100 conditional bindings per policy) causing policy-update failures that are hard to diagnose from the error message alone.
Service-account key organization policy is not enforced at the org node (only set per-project), so a new project created outside the standard pipeline can still upload/create keys.
A shared 'ci-everything' service account used across dev/staging/prod means one compromised staging workflow can reach production resources.
anti_patterns: Generating or committing any `*.json` service-account key file, including as a 'temporary' local convenience or in a `.env.example`.
Setting `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` in a workflow or Dockerfile to a path containing a checked-in or downloaded key.
Storing a service-account key as a GitHub Actions repo/org secret instead of configuring WIF.
Binding `roles/owner` or `roles/editor` to any CI-facing principal (service account or principalSet).
Writing a WIF attribute condition that only checks `assertion.repository_owner` (name-based) without also pinning `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id`.
Creating one Workload Identity Pool provider per repository instead of one provider per trust boundary with per-repo attribute conditions — burns through the providers-per-pool quota.
Hardcoding a real numeric project ID, project number, or organization ID in application code or checked-in IaC instead of injecting via environment/config.
Granting `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` or `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` at the project level when only one specific service account needs to be impersonable.
Skipping `permissions: id-token: write` and then working around the resulting failure by falling back to a key-based auth path 'just for this workflow'.
Flat project structure at the org root with no folders, mixing prod and non-prod resources under identical IAM bindings.
tools: gcloud CLI (`gcloud iam workload-identity-pools`, `gcloud iam service-accounts`) — canonical CLI for creating pools, providers, and service accounts, and for org-policy enforcement.

Terraform / OpenTofu with the `google` provider — preferred for repeatable, reviewable WIF and IAM setup as code; use `google_iam_workload_identity_pool` and `google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider` resources.
google-github-actions/auth (GitHub Action) — exchanges the GitHub OIDC token for Google credentials in a workflow run; supports Direct WIF and impersonation modes.
google-github-actions/setup-gcloud — installs and configures `gcloud`/`gsutil` in a workflow after `auth` has run.
Google Cloud Console IAM & Admin UI — for ad hoc inspection of workload identity pools, service accounts, and IAM policy bindings; not for repeatable provisioning.
Activity Analyzer (IAM Recommender) — surfaces unused service accounts and over-broad role grants for cleanup.
Cloud Audit Logs (Data Access logs for IAM and STS APIs) — required to see impersonation and token-exchange events; must be explicitly enabled.
Organization Policy Service (`gcloud resource-manager org-policies`) — enforces `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` / `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` org-wide.
Policy Analyzer / Policy Troubleshooter — diagnoses why a principal does or doesn't have effective access across the resource hierarchy.
OIDC debugger / `jwt.io` (external) — useful during setup to inspect the actual claims GitHub's OIDC token presents, to write correct attribute mappings/conditions.

deprecation_watch: Downloaded service-account JSON keys are not deprecated as a feature but are org-policy-disabled by default for organizations created after 2024-05-03 — treat key-based auth as end-of-life for any new footprint.

Firebase Admin SDK does not support WIF as of this research pass — isolate any Firebase Admin usage in its own tightly-scoped project/service-account rather than assuming universal WIF coverage across the stack.

Avoid provisioning per-repository Workload Identity Pool providers as a scaling pattern — this consumes the 200-providers-per-pool quota faster than necessary; prefer one provider per trust boundary with attribute-condition scoping.

Legacy 'Editor'/'Owner' broad primitive roles remain available but are explicitly discouraged by Google's own best-practices docs for any automation identity — expect increasing organization-policy pressure against broad role grants over time.

Watch for GitHub's OIDC token claim schema evolving (new claims added, e.g. `repository_id` was added after `repository`) — attribute mappings written against older claim sets should be revisited periodically.
identity_model: Identity in this stack is layered: (1) human operators authenticate to `gcloud`/Console via their Google identity and are granted roles through the org/folder/project IAM hierarchy, with folder-level bindings inherited downward; (2) workloads that run inside Google Cloud (Cloud Run, GKE, Cloud Functions) are attached directly to a user-managed service account and get automatic, keyless credentials from the metadata server; (3) workloads that run outside Google Cloud — critically, GitHub Actions runners — never hold a Google identity of their own. Instead, GitHub's OIDC provider issues a short-lived (5-minute) signed JWT describing the calling workflow (repo, ref, actor, event). A Workload Identity Pool Provider configured to trust `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` validates that JWT's signature and issuer, applies an attribute mapping to project selected claims into a Google-internal principal identifier, and — only if the provider's attribute condition (a CEL boolean expression) evaluates true — allows Security Token Service (STS) to mint a short-lived Google access token for that federated principal. That federated principal (`principal://...` for a single identity or `principalSet://...` for anyone matching a mapped attribute) can either hold IAM role bindings directly (Direct WIF) or be granted `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on a specific service account, which it then impersonates to obtain that service account's short-lived access token (WIF + impersonation). In both branches, no long-lived secret material ever leaves Google's control plane or GitHub's OIDC issuer — the only artifact in the workflow logs is a short-lived bearer token. IAM Conditions layer a second, independent CEL-based gate on top of any binding (resource attributes, request time, etc.), letting a single principalSet be restricted to specific resources or time windows without needing a second pool/provider. The entire model's security rests on the attribute condition being correct and specific (numeric IDs, not names) — a missing or loose condition collapses the trust boundary back to 'anyone who can trigger a GitHub Actions workflow in this org.'
threats: Confused deputy via missing/loose attribute condition: any workflow run (including from a forked PR, if the workflow trigger allows it) that satisfies an overly-broad condition can obtain the mapped IAM role's access.

Name-based attribute reuse: a GitHub repository or org name is renamed/deleted and re-registered by an attacker, and a condition keyed on `repository`/`repository_owner` (string) now matches the attacker's repo.

Token leakage in workflow logs or third-party actions: a short-lived STS/access token printed to logs or exfiltrated by a malicious third-party GitHub Action still grants access for its (short) remaining lifetime.

Overprivileged CI service account: a service account impersonated by WIF is granted broad roles 'to unblock a deploy' and becomes a high-value target if any workflow in the trusting repo is compromised (e.g. via a malicious dependency or supply-chain PR).
Fork-triggered workflow abuse: `pull_request_target` or misconfigured triggers let a fork's workflow run with the base repo's `id-token: write` permission and the parent repo's WIF trust.
Stale/unused workload identity pools, providers, or service accounts left active after a migration, expanding the attack surface with no active owner monitoring them.

Organization policy drift: a newer project created outside a standard Terraform pipeline lacks the org-level key-creation-disable policy applied correctly (e.g. policy set at wrong node, or exception granted and never revoked).

Privilege escalation via `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`/`workloadIdentityUser` granted too broadly at the project level, letting an unrelated principal impersonate any service account in the project.
Cross-environment blast radius from a shared CI service account used by both staging and production deploy workflows.
mitigations: Mandatory attribute condition on every Workload Identity Pool provider, scoped to numeric `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id`, never left empty.
IAM Condition on production-impersonation bindings restricting to `assertion.ref=='refs/heads/main'` (or equivalent) and excluding pull-request-triggered contexts.
One dedicated, minimally-scoped service account per deploy target/environment; never share a CI service account across environments.
Org policies `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` enforced at the organization node, not just per-project, with periodic policy-drift audits.
Enable Cloud Audit Logs data access logging for the IAM and Security Token Service APIs; alert on unexpected impersonation or token-exchange volume/source.

Restrict GitHub Actions workflow triggers so `id-token: write` is only granted to workflows triggered by trusted events (`push` to protected branches), never blanket-enabled on `pull_request_target` without additional gating.
Periodic Activity Analyzer / IAM Recommender review to find and disable unused service accounts, over-broad roles, and orphaned WIF providers.
Least-privilege predefined or custom roles only; no `roles/owner`/`roles/editor` on any automation-facing principal.
Branch protection + required reviews on workflow files themselves (`.github/workflows/**`) so an attacker can't modify the deploy workflow to redirect WIF-derived credentials.
Prefer Direct WIF over impersonation where the target API supports it, reducing the number of identities and bindings that must be individually audited.
agent_codegen_policy: MUST NOT generate, write, or scaffold any file matching a service-account key JSON shape (containing `"type": "service_account"`, `"private_key"`, `"client_email"`) under any circumstance, including as example/fixture content.
MUST NOT set or suggest setting `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to a file path in generated CI config, Dockerfiles, or `.env` templates.

MUST generate GitHub Actions workflows that authenticate via `google-github-actions/auth` with `workload_identity_provider` and include `permissions: id-token: write` explicitly at the job or workflow level.

MUST use placeholder identifiers (`my-project-id`, `my-org`, `my-repo`, numeric placeholders like `000000000000`) in any generated IaC or workflow snippet — never invent or reuse a real-looking project number.

MUST include a non-empty attribute condition whenever generating `gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc` or the Terraform equivalent — refuse to emit a provider resource with no `--attribute-condition`/`attribute_condition`.

MUST default to least-privilege predefined roles (never `roles/owner`/`roles/editor`) when generating IAM bindings for CI/service accounts, and flag the choice for human review if the requested role is broad.

SHOULD prefer Direct WIF (principalSet bound to a role) over service-account impersonation unless the target API/library is known to require a service-account identity (flag Firebase Admin SDK explicitly as an exception).

SHOULD generate separate service accounts/pools per environment (dev/staging/prod) rather than reusing one identity across environments, even if the user's initial request only mentions one environment.

MUST flag (not silently fix) any existing repo content it encounters that matches a service-account key shape or a `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` file reference, and recommend rotation/removal rather than assuming it's already invalid.
ci_gates: Repo secret scanner rejects commits containing a JSON blob matching `{"type": "service_account", ...}` shape.
CI lint step fails the build if any workflow YAML sets `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to a file path instead of relying on WIF-injected ADC.
CI lint step fails if a `google-github-actions/auth` step is present without a sibling `permissions: id-token: write` at job or workflow scope.
Terraform/OpenTofu plan step fails (via a policy-as-code check, e.g. OPA/Conftest) if a `google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider` resource has an empty or missing `attribute_condition`.
Terraform/OpenTofu plan step fails if any `google_project_iam_member`/`google_project_iam_binding` grants `roles/owner` or `roles/editor` to a service account or principalSet.

Periodic (weekly) scheduled job runs `gcloud iam service-accounts keys list` across all project service accounts and fails/alerts if any user-managed key exists beyond an explicitly allow-listed exception.
Periodic scheduled job verifies org policies `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`/`iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` are still `enforced: true` at the org node.
Branch protection requires review on changes to `.github/workflows/*.yml` and to Terraform files defining WIF pools/providers/IAM bindings.
observability: Cloud Audit Logs: Data Access logs enabled for `iam.googleapis.com` and `sts.googleapis.com`, forwarded to a central logging project/sink.
Alert on STS `google.identity.sts.v1.IdentityBindingService` token exchanges from unexpected principals or at unexpected volume/time-of-day.
Alert on any `iam.serviceAccounts.keys.create` or `iam.serviceAccounts.keys.upload` call anywhere in the org (should be near-zero given org policy; any hit is worth investigating).
Alert on IAM policy changes (`SetIamPolicy`) affecting WIF pools/providers or CI-facing service accounts, correlated with the acting principal.
Activity Analyzer dashboards reviewed periodically for service accounts with no recent authentication activity (candidates for disabling).
GitHub Actions workflow run logs correlated with Cloud Audit Log entries via request/operation IDs to build an end-to-end deploy audit trail.
Dashboard/alert on Workload Identity Pool provider count approaching the 200-per-pool quota, to catch the per-repo-provider anti-pattern before it causes an outage.
cost_guardrails: Workload Identity Federation, IAM role bindings, and service accounts themselves are not separately billed line items [uncertain] — cost exposure comes from the resources/APIs the granted identity can call, so guardrails should focus on the scope of granted roles rather than IAM cost itself.

Budget alerts on the projects that CI service accounts can deploy into, since a compromised or misconfigured CI identity's real cost risk is resource spend (e.g. runaway Cloud Run/BigQuery jobs), not IAM API usage.
Cap the blast radius of any single WIF-derived identity to one project or a narrow resource set, so a cost anomaly is trivially traceable to one workflow.

Avoid over-provisioning Workload Identity Pools/providers per repository (each is free but adds operational/audit overhead and quota pressure) — consolidate onto shared pools with attribute-condition scoping.
skill_scan_signals: Flag any file (any extension) whose JSON content contains the keys `"type": "service_account"` and `"private_key"` together — high-confidence committed service-account key.

Flag any occurrence of the environment variable name `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` being assigned a literal file path (not sourced from a WIF-populated runtime variable) in workflow YAML, Dockerfiles, or `.env*` files.
Flag any GitHub Actions workflow step using `google-github-actions/auth` that lacks a corresponding `permissions: id-token: write` in the same job or workflow.
Flag any Terraform/OpenTofu `google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider` resource (or `gcloud ... providers create-oidc` command) with no `attribute_condition`/`--attribute-condition` argument.

Flag any IAM binding (Terraform `google_project_iam_member`/`_binding`, or `gcloud ... add-iam-policy-binding`) granting `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or `roles/iam.securityAdmin` to a `serviceAccount:` or `principalSet://` member.
Flag any attribute condition or mapping referencing `assertion.repository` or `assertion.repository_owner` (string claims) without also referencing `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id`.

Flag any hardcoded 10-13 digit numeric string adjacent to `projects/` in code or config that isn't clearly a placeholder (real GCP project numbers are numeric; placeholders should use obviously-fake sequences like `000000000000`).
Flag any hostname in config that isn't `example.com`, `*.example.com`, or another IANA-reserved placeholder domain when the surrounding context is documentation/example code.

Flag `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create` appearing anywhere in a script, Makefile, or CI workflow — this command should not exist in a keyless architecture outside a documented, reviewed exception.
skill_module_bullets: Org/folder/project hierarchy: org at top, folders per environment, projects nested under environment folders; folders nest up to 10 levels deep and a folder holds at most 300 direct child folders.
Zero JSON service-account keys: enforce via org policy (`iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`, `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload`) plus a secret-scanning CI gate, not just convention.

GitHub Actions authenticates via `google-github-actions/auth@v3` using either Direct WIF (principalSet bound to IAM roles) or WIF + service-account impersonation (`roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser`); Firebase Admin SDK is the known exception requiring non-WIF auth.

Every Workload Identity Pool provider must carry a non-empty attribute condition; use numeric `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id` claims, never name-based `repository`/`repository_owner` alone, to avoid rename/takeover attacks.
`permissions: id-token: write` is mandatory in any workflow calling `google-github-actions/auth` — its absence is the most common setup failure.
One dedicated, least-privilege service account per deploy target/environment; never share across dev/staging/prod.
IAM Conditions (CEL) layer additional resource/time/branch restrictions on top of WIF bindings — recommended cap of ~100 conditional bindings per allow policy as a best practice, not a hard quota.
Providers-per-pool quota is 200 — architect for one provider per trust boundary with attribute-condition scoping, not one provider per repository.
Access tokens default to a 1-hour lifetime (extendable to 12 hours via org policy for specific service accounts); GitHub's own OIDC token used to bootstrap the exchange lives only 5 minutes.
checklist: Org policies `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload` are enforced at the organization node.
Folder structure exists per environment, with projects correctly nested (not flat at org root).
A Workload Identity Pool and provider exist for GitHub Actions, trusting `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
The provider's attribute condition is non-empty and keyed on numeric `repository_id`/`repository_owner_id`.
Every CI-facing service account is single-purpose, least-privilege, and scoped to one environment.
Every workflow calling `google-github-actions/auth` declares `permissions: id-token: write`.
No file in the repo matches a service-account key JSON shape; secret scanning confirms this in CI.
No `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` env var points at a checked-in or downloaded key file anywhere in the codebase or CI config.
Production-impersonation IAM bindings carry a condition restricting to the release branch and excluding PR-triggered runs.
Cloud Audit Logs data access logging is enabled for IAM and STS APIs, with alerting wired to the team's on-call channel.
A periodic (at least monthly) review has run via Activity Analyzer / IAM Recommender to catch unused service accounts or stale WIF providers.
Workload identity pool provider count is tracked against the 200-per-pool quota and architected to stay well under it.
conflicts_noted: The official `resource-manager/docs/quotas` and `iam/docs/conditions-overview` pages did not explicitly state a numeric limit on workload identity pools per project or a fixed service-accounts-per-project quota — these are marked [uncertain] rather than asserted. The `google-github-actions/auth` README (primary OSS source) and Google's official WIF docs agree on Direct WIF vs impersonation-via-service-account as the two supported patterns; no conflicts found between sources on core mechanics.
